name: Liberty Square
intro: Liberty Square (Szabadság tér) is a broad public square in Lipótváros, created after the Újépület barracks were demolished in 1897 and named in 1900. Two large buildings by Ignác Alpár, the former Stock Exchange Palace and the National Bank headquarters, frame it, while its monuments, from a Soviet memorial to a Reagan statue, record a century of Hungarian politics.
about: Liberty Square lies in Lipótváros, in the fifth district, a short walk from the Parliament and St. Stephen's Basilica. It is better understood as a civic space than as a single sight: a large public square with mature trees, a fountain and a dense collection of monuments, surrounded by monumental buildings that include the United States Embassy.

The architecture is the main reason to stop. The former Stock Exchange Palace at number 17, designed by Ignác Alpár and built between 1902 and 1907, has a rusticated base, Ionic pilasters rising through three storeys and a central pediment flanked by two towers, approached by a wide flight of steps. Alpár also designed the National Bank headquarters at numbers 8 and 9, an eclectic neo-Baroque building handed over in 1905.

The square doubles as an outdoor record of changing politics. A Soviet memorial of 1946 stands here, now surrounded by protective railings after repeated vandalism, alongside a statue of the American general Harry Hill Bandholtz, a Ronald Reagan statue unveiled in 2011 and a statue of George H. W. Bush unveiled in 2020. The memorial to the German occupation, unveiled in 2014, remains contested, and several of these monuments mean quite different things to different visitors.

Most of the surrounding buildings are working institutions, so the visit is mainly about exteriors and the public space. The National Bank is a central bank headquarters, and a report from February 2026 describes the Stock Exchange Palace as empty, with reconstruction about to begin and its future use not yet announced. Check current notices and the state of the memorials before you go, because both can change.
tips: Treat the Stock Exchange Palace and the National Bank as exterior sights: neither is described by its sources as a visitor attraction, and the Stock Exchange Palace may be affected by building works.

Read the plaques and look at each memorial on its own terms. The German occupation memorial and its counter-memorial of photographs are the subject of an ongoing public debate, and the Soviet memorial is protected by railings.
Combine the square with the Parliament and St. Stephen's Basilica, both a short walk away, or with the nearby Gresham Palace.
For photographs, a wide lens helps with the long façade of the Stock Exchange Palace, whose central towers and pediment are its most distinctive feature.

history.intro: The square exists because of a demolition. Its story runs from an Austrian-era barracks, through a district of Alpár-designed financial buildings, to the memorials of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries.

sections.heading: From the Újépület barracks to Szabadság tér
paragraphs: According to Hungarian Wikipedia, construction of the Újépület (New Building) began on the site in 1786 to designs by Isidore Canevale, overseen by János Hild, and the building later served as a prison, an artillery barracks and a military academy. After the revolution and war of independence of 1848–49 it was again a prison, and Lajos Batthyány, Hungary's first responsible prime minister, was executed there in 1849.
The Újépület was demolished in 1897, and the square that replaced it was named Szabadság tér in 1900, after the 1848–49 war of independence.

sections.heading: Alpár's Stock Exchange and National Bank
paragraphs: The national heritage register dates the Stock Exchange Palace to 1902–1907, built to plans by Ignác Alpár as Budapest's commodity and securities exchange; Hungarian Wikipedia gives a wider span beginning in 1897, so sources differ on the start. A 2026 report says the building housed Hungarian Television from 1955 to 2009 and has stood empty for nearly twenty years.

The National Bank's press office dates its headquarters to 1902–1905, built as the Budapest branch of the Austro-Hungarian Bank. The Hungarian National Bank was founded on 24 June 1924 and has used the building ever since; the same release describes post-war alterations and a full reconstruction timed for the 2024 centenary.

sections.heading: Monuments and disputes since 1945
paragraphs: Hungarian Wikipedia records the Soviet memorial of 1946 and the Bandholtz statue, erected in 1936, removed in 1949 and re-erected in 1989. The Reagan statue followed in 2011.

The German occupation memorial was unveiled on 20 July 2014 and provoked protests. English Wikipedia describes it as showing Hungary as an angel attacked by a German eagle, and reports the criticism that this symbolism obscures Hungary's own part in the Holocaust; a counter-memorial of photographs of Hungarians deported to Auschwitz was set up in front of it the same year.

name: Fiumei Road National Graveyard (Kerepesi Cemetery)
intro: The Fiumei Road National Graveyard, long known as Kerepesi Cemetery, is Hungary's national pantheon, a 56-hectare burial ground in Józsefváros that opened in 1849. Its arcades, mausoleums and artists' plots hold statesmen, writers and composers, among them Batthyány, Deák, Kossuth, Jókai and Ady, and it is a place for quiet walking.
about: The Fiumei Road National Graveyard is a cemetery, a memorial park and an open-air museum of funerary art at once. The site covers 56 hectares, of which 25 are landscaped according to Hungarian Wikipedia, and its tree cover gives it the feel of an arboretum. Both names are in use: Kerepesi is the old street-based name, and Fiumei úti sírkert is the current official one.

The most prominent graves belong to the national figures of the nineteenth century. Lajos Batthyány, Ferenc Deák and Lajos Kossuth each have a mausoleum, and the Kossuth mausoleum is described by the heritage institute as the largest grave monument in Hungary. Writers and artists lie in their own plots; the poet Endre Ady and the novelist Mór Jókai are among those commemorated with monuments, and arcades completed in 1908 are another notable feature.

Walking here is quieter and slower than at most Budapest sights. Many tombs are significant works by well-known architects and sculptors, and the separate plots for artists, the Jacobins and the heroes of 1848 and 1956 give the layout a clear historical logic. The official site lists themed guided walks, for instance on prime ministers' graves, mausoleums and scientists, as well as memorial events around All Saints' Day.

The cemetery is run by the National Heritage Institute (Nemzeti Örökség Intézete) and is still a working burial ground, so respect for mourners comes first. The official page states that the Workers' Movement Pantheon is closed to visitors for an indefinite period because of its technical condition, and that mausoleum interiors are visited only with a member of staff, so look at the page before planning.
tips: Check the official page of the National Heritage Institute for current visiting conditions, any notices and the guided walks on offer; mausoleum interiors and the Workers' Movement Pantheon are not part of ordinary walk-in visits.
Behave as in any working cemetery: keep voices low, stay on the paths and do not touch or lean on monuments. Burials and funerals still take place here.
The official site sets rules on photography and filming, so read them before bringing a camera, and ask staff if you are unsure.
Plan a route in advance: the site covers 56 hectares, and the mausoleums, the artists' plots and the arcades are in different parts of it.

history.intro: The cemetery began as a practical measure and grew into a national pantheon. Its history is closely tied to the funerals of the figures it holds.

sections.heading: From city cemetery to honoured ground
paragraphs: The Pest city magistrate chose the site on the Kerepes road for a new public cemetery in 1847, and Hungarian Wikipedia records its official opening on 1 April 1849. The heritage institute notes that the main aim was to relieve the older cemeteries, and Hungarian Wikipedia adds that Pest citizens were at first reluctant to use it. Mihály Vörösmarty, buried in 1855, was among the first notable burials.

In 1885 the capital declared it an honorary cemetery (dísztemető). In 1956 it was declared a national pantheon, and in 2013 Parliament made it a national memorial site. Management passed to the National Heritage Institute on 1 May 2016.

sections.heading: The great mausoleums
paragraphs: Lajos Batthyány was reburied here on 9 June 1870, and his mausoleum, designed by Albert Schickedanz, was completed in 1874. Ferenc Deák was buried on 3 February 1876; his mausoleum, designed by Kálmán Gerster, was built in 1884–1887 according to Hungarian Wikipedia.

Lajos Kossuth's funeral in 1894 was organised by the capital rather than the state. He was reburied in his own mausoleum on 25 November 1909, completed that year to designs by Gerster. The arcades were completed in 1908 to designs by Lajos Gerle and Árpád Hegedűs.

sections.heading: Twentieth-century changes
paragraphs: Jókai was buried in 1904 and Ady in 1919. The cemetery suffered damage and looting in the siege of Budapest, and plans to close it were drawn up in the early 1950s, but on 17 May 1956 it was declared a closed, protected cemetery and national pantheon. A central memorial to the 1956 revolution was unveiled in 1999. Hungarian Wikipedia gives 1958 for the completion of the Workers' Movement Pantheon, while the institute says it was handed over in 1959, so the sources differ on that detail.

name: Kozma Street Jewish Cemetery
intro: The Kozma Street Jewish Cemetery, beside the New Public Cemetery in eastern Budapest, is Hungary's largest Jewish burial ground, with about 300,000 people buried there. Hungarian sources date its opening to 1893. It is known for a Moorish-style ceremonial hall, Art Nouveau family mausoleums and tombs, and it is a working cemetery that calls for respect.
about: The Kozma Street cemetery lies on the eastern edge of the city, in the tenth district, next to the municipal New Public Cemetery. It is the largest Jewish cemetery in Hungary and is still in use by the Budapest Jewish Community, which belongs to the federation Mazsihisz. Visiting means a journey away from the central districts and a long, slow walk through a very large site.

Near the entrance stands the ceremonial hall, a white Moorish-style building designed by Vilmos Freund; its dates differ between sources (see History). Beyond it, the cemetery is notable for its sculpted and Art Nouveau tombs, which are unusual in a Jewish burial ground. The Schmidl family mausoleum was designed by Béla Lajta with Zsolnay ceramics, and the Gries and Schmidl mausoleums are listed monuments. Other graves hold figures such as the aviation pioneer Viktor Wittmann, the writer Sándor Bródy and Alfréd Hajós, Hungary's first Olympic champion.

The character is that of a sacred place, not of a sightseeing stop. Overgrown graves are not necessarily neglected: one account explains that, under Jewish custom, plants on a grave are a sign of respect and should not be removed. Many graves are nonetheless in poor condition because no relatives survive. After the Second World War a memorial wall for the victims of the Holocaust, designed by Hajós, was added.

For visitors, it rewards unhurried time spent on a few graves and on the atmosphere. The Mazsihisz database page gives the address and contact details, and it is the page to check for access arrangements, which can change.
tips: Check the Mazsihisz database page, or phone the contact numbers it lists, for current access arrangements and days when the cemetery is shut, before travelling out.
Dress and behave as you would in a place of worship, keep your voice low, do not remove plants or stones from graves, and ask the cemetery staff about any expectations such as head coverings.

The site is far larger than it first looks. An account of a three-hour guided walk reports that it still did not cover everything, so choose a few things to see, such as the ceremonial hall and the Lajta mausoleums.
Use the street address, Kozma utca 6, in a map or taxi app to find the entrance.

history.intro: The cemetery was created when Pest's older Jewish burial grounds were filling up. Its later history includes decades of neglect and a slow restoration.

sections.heading: Founding in the 1890s
paragraphs: According to Hungarian Wikipedia, Budapest's municipal assembly set aside land at Keresztúridűlő in 1883 for the New Public Cemetery. In 1891, at the request of the Pest Chevra Kadisha, it approved a separate Jewish cemetery next to it. The cemetery opened in 1893 and took its name from the street at its entrance. Some English-language sources give 1891 as the founding year, which matches the approval date.

The first burials were largely remains moved from the older Váci út cemetery. The ceremonial hall, designed by Vilmos Freund, is dated 1894–1895 by Hungarian Wikipedia, while two other accounts give 1891, so that date remains uncertain.

sections.heading: Mausoleums, memorials and later management
paragraphs: Béla Lajta's Schmidl mausoleum dates from the early 1900s and was renovated in the late 1990s. The cemetery was run by the Pest Israelite Community, and since 1950 by the Budapest Jewish Community; Hungarian Wikipedia gives about 300,000 burials.
After 1945 Alfréd Hajós designed a memorial wall for the victims of the Holocaust, which the blog Hype and Hyper dates to 1949.

sections.heading: Neglect and restoration
paragraphs: Until the 2010s the site was largely cut off and overgrown, leaving outer sections hard to reach. Since 2016 the non-profit Zsidó Temetők Barátai has been working on restoration, slowly according to Hungarian Wikipedia, and in 2023 the German group Aktion Sühnezeichen Friedensdienst carried out clean-up work with the Hungarian Jewish Cultural Association. The Brüll family crypt was renovated in 2017.

name: Former Postal Savings Bank (Hold Street)
intro: The former Royal Hungarian Postal Savings Bank on Hold utca is a Hungarian Secession landmark designed by Ödön Lechner and Sándor Baumgarten, dated 1900 in the heritage register and handed over in 1901. Its ornamental façade, ceramic tiles and beehive motifs make it a rewarding exterior sight, and it is now the headquarters of the Hungarian State Treasury.
about: The Postal Savings Bank at Hold utca 4 is one of the best-known buildings of Ödön Lechner, the architect who sought a distinctly Hungarian form of Secession. It is a four-storey building with three street fronts, which carries the addresses Hold utca 4, Kiss Ernő utca 4 and Perczel Mór utca 3, and it is protected as a monument. The Lechner Knowledge Centre treats it as the place where Lechner's restrained, clean-formed style is most fully realised.

What you see from the street is the decoration. Hungarian Wikipedia lists floral motifs, coloured ceramic tiles and majolica, octagonal columns on the corner and central projecting sections with tower finials of Indian inspiration, and golden-yellow beehives on the gable, a symbol of saving and thrift. Accounts differ on how much of the original roofing survives: Hungarian Wikipedia describes a steep roof with Zsolnay ceramic tiles, while a 2024 article says the iconic hive-like roof was later replaced.

Inside, the former cash hall had a glass dome that Hungarian Wikipedia calls an architectural novelty; it was removed in the 1930s after weather damage. A 2024 article reports that the hall's reconstruction was completed in 2023, and that the dome, by the artist Waltherr Gida, has not been rebuilt.

The building is a working government office, the headquarters of the Hungarian State Treasury, and the sources consulted do not describe regular public visiting, so treat it as an exterior sight. It stands very close to Liberty Square, and the Museum of Applied Arts lists it among five Lechner buildings in Hungary's UNESCO tentative-list nomination.
tips: View the building from the street and look up: the gable, the ceramic roof details and the tower finials are the details that repay attention.
Because it is a government office, do not assume you can go inside. Check the Hungarian State Treasury's own pages for any public event before travelling.
Walk on to Liberty Square, a few minutes away, to see Ignác Alpár's Stock Exchange Palace and National Bank, or on to the Parliament and the Gresham Palace.
The building wraps around a corner and faces several streets, so walk round it to see each front.

history.intro: The bank was created to hold the savings of ordinary Hungarians, and its headquarters became one of the most admired and discussed buildings of its day.

sections.heading: A competition and a Secession design
paragraphs: Hungarian Wikipedia says the Royal Hungarian Postal Savings Bank was established in 1895 and that a tender for its Budapest headquarters was announced in 1899, which Lechner's design won; Sándor Baumgarten is named as co-designer. The heritage register lists the work as Hungarian Secession by Lechner and Baumgarten, dated 1900.

sections.heading: Construction and early recognition
paragraphs: Construction took about a year and a half, according to Hungarian Wikipedia, while a 2024 article says the building was completed in 1901 within about a year, so the sources differ slightly. Hungarian Wikipedia reports that the Hungarian Artists' Association awarded the building its Grand Gold Medal in 1900, and that it was handed over in 1901.

sections.heading: Changes and later use
paragraphs: In the 1930s the weather-damaged glass dome of the cash hall was removed, and Lechner's interior furnishings were largely replaced, so that only two benches survive, according to Hungarian Wikipedia. The cash hall was boarded up for decades, a 2024 article reports, before its reconstruction was completed in 2023. The Hungarian State Treasury now occupies the building, and it appears among five Lechner buildings in the UNESCO tentative-list nomination.

name: Római-part Riverside
address: Danube bank in Óbuda-Békásmegyer, Budapest III (Rómaifürdő area)
intro: The Római-part is a stretch of Danube bank in the third district, about 5 km long according to English Wikipedia, with a pebbly natural shore, a narrow promenade, surviving boathouses and riverside eateries. It is a local recreation area for walking, cycling and watersports, with a long history of rowing and weekend life by the river.
about: The Római-part is the northern Danube bank of Óbuda-Békásmegyer, a long strip where the river, a pebbly shoreline and a narrow promenade sit between water and the road. English Wikipedia places it between the mouths of the Barát and Aranyhegyi creeks and gives its length as about 5 km. The Budapest community-planning vision of 2021 names the natural gravel shore, patches of floodplain woodland and the surviving boathouses among its chief assets.

What visitors do here is simple: walk or cycle along the promenade, sit at a riverside eatery, watch rowers and boats, or step down onto the shore. English Wikipedia calls it a local recreation area, and the vision document values its mix of city and nature-like riverbank. The riverside eateries are popular mainly from spring to autumn.

The shore is not one single, polished attraction. The same 2021 document describes a narrow promenade, many privately owned plots, run-down boathouse infrastructure and eateries that work on short-term permits, which is why the character is rough and informal. This entry covers the promenade and shore; the nearby Lupa Beach and the Római Open-Air Bath are described separately.

Practically, treat the Római-part as an outdoor outing rather than a timetabled sight. The HÉV suburban railway stops at Rómaifürdő, and the city's planning pages are the place to check for works, planning decisions and flood-protection plans that could affect access.
tips: Check the City of Budapest's Római-part pages for current planning and any works on the promenade or shore before you set out; flood protection and regulation of the area have been under discussion for years.
Wear sturdy shoes: the shore is pebbly and uneven, and the narrow promenade is shared by walkers, cyclists and people heading to the eateries.
Combine the walk with the nearby Lupa Beach or Római Open-Air Bath, which have their own entries.
Keep to marked paths and take away your rubbish: the vision document lists waste on the shore and promenade among the area's problems.
Prefer a clear day for photographs of the river and the wooded bank, and keep a safe distance from the water's edge when levels are high.

history.intro: The name points to the Roman past, but most of what shaped today's shore dates from the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, when rowing, bathing and weekend houses made it a popular leisure area.

sections.heading: From Roman Aquincum to the Bivalyos csárda
paragraphs: The city's 2021 vision document explains that the name recalls Roman Aquincum, which lay to the south, and that the Romans built a bath over the thermal springs at today's strand in the second century. In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries the road linking Óbuda with Szentendre ran here, buffalo dealers used the ford, and the Bivalyos csárda, which opened in 1798 beside the market ground, still stands, although the document describes it as closed. Floating mills worked on the river before steam mills turned the shore towards inns and fish eateries.

sections.heading: Rowing, boathouses and the golden decades
paragraphs: The document dates the first Danube rowing regatta, modelled on English practice, to 1842, and notes that the opening of the HÉV suburban railway in 1888 boosted the area's popularity. After 1900 boathouses, pontoon baths, buffets and garden restaurants appeared, and the document calls the 1920s and 1930s the area's first heyday. In 1968 it counts 91 holiday homes and 15 boathouses in operation.

The bathing places were shut in 1973 because of declining water quality, which many date as the start of the area's decline. After the 1990s privatisation most holiday homes and boathouses disappeared.

sections.heading: Flood protection and the vision for the future
paragraphs: After the flood of 1953 an embankment was built along Nánási út and Királyok útja. In the 2000s plans for a mobile flood barrier on the bank were stopped by years of civic opposition. The city and the third district began community planning in 2020, and its vision document, published in March 2021, sets out priorities for the next twenty years and says the flood-protection question was still unresolved.
